title: Modules (C++20) and import std (C++23)
summary: **Modules** replace header files: you `export` what is public and `import` it elsewhere. A module is compiled **once**, leaks no macros and has no include-order problems. C++23's `import std;` brings in the whole standard library in one line.
markdown:
## What is wrong with headers `#include` is textual substitution ([[1.08 Multiple Files and Headers]]). That simple model has real costs. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph H["#include: the text is pasted in"] direction LR h1["a.cpp"] -->|"re-parses iostream,
vector, string ..."| hh["tens of thousands of lines,
in EVERY source file"] h2["b.cpp"] -->|"and again"| hh end subgraph M["import: compiled once"] direction LR m0["math.cppm"] -->|"compiled once"| bmi["a binary description
of the module"] bmi --> m1["a.cpp: import math;"] bmi --> m2["b.cpp: import math;"] end ``` | | Headers | Modules | |---|---|---| | Processed | Every time one is included | Once | | Macros defined inside | Leak into every file that includes it | Stay inside | | The order of inclusion | Can change the meaning | Is irrelevant | | Include guards | Required | Not needed | | Private helpers | Visible to everyone, by convention "do not touch" | Invisible unless exported | | Build time | Dominated by re-parsing | Often much lower | ## Writing a module ### math.cppm: the interface ```cpp module; // the global module fragment: old-style includes go here #include export module math; // this file is the interface of module "math" export namespace math { constexpr double pi{ 3.14159265358979 }; double circleArea(double radius) { return pi * radius * radius; } template T square(T x) { return x * x; } } double helper() { return 42.0; } // not exported: importers cannot see it ``` ### main.cpp ```cpp import std; // C++23: the entire standard library import math; int main() { std::println("{}", math::circleArea(2.0)); // helper(); error: not visible outside the module return 0; } ``` | Line | Meaning | |---|---| | `export module math;` | Declares a **module interface unit**: the file that defines what module `math` offers | | `export` on a declaration or a block | Makes it visible to importers | | `import math;` | Makes the exported names of `math` available | | `module;` followed by `#include`s | The **global module fragment**, for headers that must still be included textually | Everything not exported has **module linkage**: it is usable throughout the module and invisible outside it. That is true encapsulation at the level of a library, which headers never offered. Templates may live in a module interface and be exported like anything else. ### Interface and implementation As with a header and a source file, a module can separate what it declares from how it is implemented. ```cpp // geometry.cppm: the interface export module geometry; export double area(double width, double height); ``` ```cpp // geometry.cpp: an implementation unit module geometry; double area(double width, double height) { return width * height; } ``` A change to the implementation unit does not force importers to recompile. ### Partitions A large module can be divided into **partitions**, which are internal to it. ```cpp // physics.cppm export module game:physics; export double gravity(); ``` ```cpp // game.cppm export module game; export import :physics; // re-export the partition ``` Users write `import game;`. The partitions are an organisational detail they never see. ## `import std;` `import std;` makes the whole standard library available. Because the library is compiled once into a module, importing all of it is typically **faster** than including `` alone. `import std.compat;` additionally provides the C library names in the global namespace. ## Building Modules introduce an ordering requirement that headers did not have: a module's interface must be compiled **before** anything that imports it. The build system has to discover those dependencies by scanning the sources. ```cmake cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.30) project(ModuleDemo LANGUAGES CXX) set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23) set(CMAKE_CXX_MODULE_STD ON) add_executable(app main.cpp) target_sources(app PUBLIC FILE_SET CXX_MODULES FILES math.cppm) ``` CMake 3.28 and later handle the scanning, with the Ninja generator or Visual Studio. The interface file's extension is a convention: `.cppm` for Clang and GCC, `.ixx` for Visual Studio. | Toolchain | Status | |---|---| | Microsoft's compiler | The most mature support | | Clang 17 and later, GCC 14 and later | Work well with CMake and Ninja | | Third-party libraries | Most still ship headers only | > [!note] You need both > Headers are not going away. Existing libraries use them, and a module can still include them in its global module fragment. Know both models: write new code as modules where your tools allow, and expect to consume headers for years. Xenon compiles each task as plain source files with headers, so the exercises in this course do not use modules. This lesson is preparation for your own projects. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does `export` do in a module? - It writes the module to a file + It makes a declaration visible to the module's importers - It makes the module's macros available to importers - It compiles the module into a library > Only exported declarations are seen by importers. Unexported helpers are invisible outside the module. ? Do macros defined in a module affect its importers? - Yes, like a header - Only if they are exported + No, modules do not export macros - Only macros defined before `export module` > Importing a module never brings in its macros, which is one of the ways modules are cleaner than headers. ? Why are modules faster to build than headers? - Because modules contain less code - Because modules are compiled in parallel - Because modules skip type checking + Its interface is compiled once, not re-parsed per file > Each `#include` pastes and re-parses the header text. An `import` loads an already compiled interface. ? What is the global module fragment for? + Including ordinary headers before the module declaration - Declaring global variables shared by all modules - Exporting every declaration at once - Listing which modules to import > It starts with `module;` and holds `#include` lines whose contents should not become part of the module. ```
ideas:
These need a compiler and CMake on your own machine.
1. Convert a multi-file maths library into a module with an interface unit and an implementation unit.
2. Time a clean build of twenty files that each include `<iostream>`, `<vector>`, `<map>` and `<algorithm>`, against the same files using `import std;`.
3. Show that a `#define` inside a module does not reach its importers.

cards.q: What does `export` do in a module?
cards.a:
It makes a declaration visible to the module's importers

Only exported declarations are seen by importers. Unexported helpers are invisible outside the module.

cards.q: Do macros defined in a module affect its importers?
cards.a:
No, modules do not export macros

Importing a module never brings in its macros, which is one of the ways modules are cleaner than headers.

cards.q: Why are modules faster to build than headers?
cards.a:
Its interface is compiled once, not re-parsed per file

Each `#include` pastes and re-parses the header text. An `import` loads an already compiled interface.

cards.q: What is the global module fragment for?
cards.a:
Including ordinary headers before the module declaration

It starts with `module;` and holds `#include` lines whose contents should not become part of the module.
